title: Unpacking the Determinants of Financial Resilience in the Philippines
venue: Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Discussion Paper Series
tldr: Machine learning models applied to Philippine Global Findex data reveal that income quintile, saving behavior, and gender are the top predictors of financial resilience, with demographics providing higher predictive value than financial access indicators.
problem_and_motivation: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed financial vulnerabilities in Philippine households through health shocks and income losses, deepening existing inequalities. While financial inclusion is a stated national policy goal, research on what makes Filipinos financially resilient remains limited. Determining the most important environmental factors that build financial resilience would help policymakers design better-targeted interventions for the financially vulnerable.
approach: Used World Bank Global Findex survey data for the Philippines from 2017 (n=980) and 2021 (n=992) after dropping missing observations.
Constructed a financial resilience binary variable based on respondents' self-reported ability to gather emergency funds within 30 days equivalent to 5% of GNI per capita.

Selected 23 predictive attributes across five categories following Salignac et al.'s Multidimensional Financial Resilience Framework: economic resources, financial resources, financial knowledge and behavior, social capital, and demographics.
Applied Logistic LASSO Regression to identify sparse predictor sets by zeroing out irrelevant coefficients via L1 penalty with standardized features.
Built Decision Tree models with varied hyperparameters including maximum tree depth, minimum samples per leaf/split, and cost-complexity pruning.
Introduced Random Forest and Linear Discriminant Analysis as benchmark models to compare against the more interpretable classifiers.
Evaluated models using accuracy, ROC curves, confusion matrices, and feature importance rankings, with 75-25 train-test splits.
Chose final models for inference based on highest true negative rates and lowest false positives to maximize coverage of financially vulnerable individuals.
findings: num: Income quintile, saving behavior, and gender emerged as the top predictors of financial resilience across both 2017 and 2021 survey rounds.
num: Random Forest achieved the best accuracy for 2017 data at 65.3%, while Decision Tree (alpha=0.015) achieved 68.1% for 2021 data.
num: All tested models yielded test accuracy below 70%, highlighting the need for more granular survey data.
num: Financial account ownership improved from 34.3% in 2017 to 56.8% in 2021, while mobile money account ownership leapt from 4.4% to 30.2%.
num: Online transactions surged from 8.8% in 2017 to 51.1% in 2021, while online payments rose from 9% to 51%.
num: The gender gap in financial resilience widened from 2017 (females 46.1%, males 53.6%) to 2021 (females 51.8%, males 68.6%).
num: Tertiary education jumped from minimal coefficient in 2017 to second only to income quintile in predictive power for 2021.
num: Age was strongly negatively associated with financial resilience in 2017 but became uninformative in 2021.
Saving behavior was important for lower-income respondents, while saving for retirement mattered most for higher-income respondents.
Medical borrowing showed a stronger negative association with financial resilience in 2021 compared to 2017, likely linked to pandemic health shocks.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: Financial resilience self-ratings for 2017 and 2021 → Financial resilience is roughly balanced in both survey rounds.
Figure 2: Financial resilience by age → Respondents aged 20-40 showed higher resilience in 2017; those under 25 less resilient in 2021.
Figure 4: Financial resilience by income → Higher-income households consistently reported higher resilience; poorest 40% saw decline from 2017 to 2021.
Figure 5: Financial resilience by income quintile and education → Educated individuals tend to be more financially resilient and belong to higher socioeconomic classes.
Figure 8: ROC curve across models → All models performed better than 50% chance but far from ideal; Random Forest best for 2017, LDA and LASSO best for 2021.
Figure 10: Logistic and LASSO regression coefficients → Income quintile and gender (female) are consistently strong predictors; tertiary education rose in importance from 2017 to 2021.
Figure 11: Decision trees with highest true negative rates → Income quintile is the root split; saving behavior important for 2017 but education replaces it in 2021.
Figure 12: Feature importance across decision tree and random forest models → Income quintile is the top predictor in both years; other important features differ by survey round.

definitions.definition: The ability to deal with financial shocks, measured as the capacity to gather emergency funds within 30 days equivalent to 5% of GNI per capita.
The accessibility, usage, and quality of financial products and services.
Over-indebtedness, falling behind on utility payments, insufficient discretionary income, and susceptibility to financial shocks.
A logistic regression model with L1 penalty that shrinks irrelevant coefficient estimates to zero for variable selection.
A similarity measure for binary attributes calculated as the proportion of exact matches between two variables.
Salignac et al.'s framework comprising four components: economic resources, financial resources, financial knowledge and behavior, and social capital.
A World Bank database measuring financial inclusion and financial resilience through nationally representative surveys of adults in over 140 economies.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a comparative analysis of machine learning models for predicting financial resilience in the Philippines using World Bank Global Findex data from 2017 and 2021. It identifies income quintile, saving behavior, and gender as the most important predictors, demonstrating that demographic factors have higher predictive value for financial resilience than financial access indicators. The study contextualizes findings against existing financial inclusion literature and highlights that the COVID-19 pandemic deepened financial inequalities along income, gender, and educational lines. The paper provides policymakers with baseline information on the determinants of financial resilience and supports the design of targeted interventions for the financially vulnerable.
directly_justifies: Demographics provide higher predictive value for financial resilience than financial access indicators.
Income quintile, saving behavior, and gender are the top predictors in both 2017 and 2021.
Financial inclusion does not necessarily translate to financial resilience.
The COVID-19 pandemic widened the financial resilience gap between income classes, genders, and educational attainment.
All tested models yielded test accuracy below 70%, indicating the need for more granular survey data.
limits: The narrow proxy measure for financial resilience (ability to raise emergency funds) does not capture the full multidimensional concept.
The predominantly binary nature of Global Findex variables limits model accuracy.
Missing demographic variables such as geographic location and occupation reduce predictive power.
The shift from face-to-face to phone-based surveys in 2021 may have excluded respondents without phone access.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals) was flagged as relevant at high level for financial structure (1.B) and financial behavior (1.C), and medium for demographics (1.A), since the paper analyzes Filipino adult demographics and financial behaviors as predictors. Domain 4 (Existing Personal Finance Systems) was flagged at medium for landscape (4.A) and high for limitations (4.B), as the paper contextualizes the Philippine financial inclusion landscape and identifies gaps between access and resilience. Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) was flagged at high for both profiles (5.A) and classification approaches (5.C), as the paper classifies individuals as resilient or vulnerable using ML. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged at high for 6.A, as predictive modeling of financial resilience is the paper's core contribution. Domain 10 (Data Privacy) was flagged at low for 10.B due to the brief discussion of self-reporting bias. Domains 2 (Culturally Specific Financial Practices), 3 (Expense Categorization), 7 (Budgeting Strategies), 8 (Anomaly Detection), 9 (Mobile-First Design), 11 (Engagement Dynamics), 12 (Evaluation Frameworks), 13 (Savings/Debt Goals), and 14 (Synthetic Data/ML Serving) were considered and rejected as the paper does not address these subtopics.

limitations: The narrow proxy measure for financial resilience (ability to raise emergency funds within 30 days) does not capture the full multidimensional concept of financial resilience.
The predominantly binary nature of Global Findex variables limits model accuracy and the ability to detect nuanced relationships.
Missing demographic variables such as geographic location, occupation, and industry reduce the models' predictive power.
The shift from face-to-face to phone-based surveys in 2021 may have excluded lower-income and less-educated respondents without phone access, affecting generalizability.
Self-reporting bias may arise from respondents incorrectly recalling or withholding information they deem shameful.
All models yielded test accuracy below 70%, indicating that several unmeasured factors influence financial resilience.
The study does not establish causal links between identified predictors and financial resilience.
[unacknowledged] The sample size of approximately 1,000 respondents per survey round may be insufficient for complex ML models with 23 predictors.
remember_this: Income quintile, saving behavior, and gender are the most consistent predictors of financial resilience in the Philippines.
Financial inclusion does not necessarily translate to financial resilience, as demographic factors dominate predictive models.
All ML models tested yielded accuracy below 70%, suggesting significant unmeasured determinants of financial resilience.
The COVID-19 pandemic widened financial resilience gaps along income, gender, and educational lines.
Tertiary education rose from minimal importance in 2017 to second only to income quintile in 2021.
